CausalChain: High-fat diet/obesity -> Gut microbiota dysbiosis -> Increased production of hydrophobic secondary bile acids (DCA, LCA) -> Activation of TGR5/FXR receptors (plus inflammatory co-signals) -> Epigenetic modifications (altered histone marks, DNA methylation, miRNA expression) -> Induction of cancer stem cell phenotype -> Promotion of colorectal carcinogenesis
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that a high-fat diet leads to dysbiosis of the gut microbiota, resulting in an increased production of hydrophobic secondary bile acids. These bile acids, coupled with an inflammatory environment, activate bile acid receptors TGR5 and FXR in colonic epithelial cells. The receptor activation, potentially synergized by inflammatory cytokines, induces specific epigenetic alterations—including modifications in histone acetylation and methylation, changes in DNA methyltransferase activity, and dysregulation of microRNA profiles—that drive the colonic cells toward a cancer stem cell phenotype. This epigenetic reprogramming underlies the initiation and progression of colorectal cancer. Our approach leverages state-of-the-art multi-omics profiling and CRISPR-dCas9 epigenetic editing tools to dissect and potentially reverse these molecular events in both preclinical in vitro and in vivo models.
Abstract: We propose that a high‐fat diet induces gut microbiota dysbiosis, which shifts bile acid metabolism toward an increased production of hydrophobic secondary bile acids such as deoxycholic and lithocholic acids. These bile acids, in concert with an inflammatory milieu characteristic of high-fat diet intake, trigger the activation of TGR5 and FXR receptors in colonic epithelial cells. Activation of these receptors not only induces conventional proliferative and inflammatory signaling but also reprograms the epigenetic landscape—specifically altering histone modification patterns, DNA methylation profiles, and microRNA expression. Such epigenetic alterations facilitate a transition of colonic epithelial cells to a cancer stem cell (CSC) phenotype, thereby promoting the initiation and progression of colorectal cancer. Technologically, this hypothesis can be probed and refined through integrated multi-omics analyses and targeted manipulation using CRISPR-dCas9 based epigenetic editing, providing both mechanistic insight and a platform for validating potential therapeutic interventions.
Orignal_vs_New: The original hypothesis proposed that a high‐fat diet alters gut microbiota leading to an increase in hydrophobic secondary bile acids, which activate TGR5/FXR-mediated epigenetic reprogramming to induce a cancer stem cell phenotype in colon cells, thereby promoting colorectal cancer. The revised hypothesis maintains the same causal chain but expands and refines several key points: (1) It integrates the role of an inflammatory environment that synergizes with bile acid receptor activation, addressing observations that inflammation and oxidative stress are major drivers in the process; (2) It specifies the types of epigenetic modifications involved, such as changes in histone modifications, DNA methylation, and microRNA profiles, rather than a general statement of 'epigenetic reprogramming'; (3) It outlines practical modern experimental approaches by incorporating multi-omics analyses and CRISPR-dCas9 epigenetic editing to enhance both the testability and translational potential of the hypothesis. These refinements directly correspond to the original causal steps while addressing critical gaps highlighted in the review comments.
